title: A no-go theorem for privacy in distributed sensing using Gaussian states
abstract: In the discrete variable setting, entangled resource states allow a set of parties to learn a global function of a set of spatially separated systems, whilst keeping the local parameters of those systems completely private. In the continuous variable setting, distributed sensing has been carried out using Gaussian resource states, but without the same guarantees about privacy. Here, we show that perfect privacy is impossible to achieve for any distributed sensing protocol that uses Gaussian states as a resource. We also introduce a measure of relative privacy, bounding the degree to which any Gaussian distributed sensing protocol can keep local parameters hidden.
summary: This paper establishes a no-go theorem proving that perfect privacy cannot be achieved in distributed quantum sensing when Gaussian states are used as resources. The authors develop and analyze a quantitative measure called relative privacy to characterize the maximum achievable information leakage instead of absolute secrecy. This result sets fundamental theoretical bounds for quantum sensing protocols using continuous variables.
main_problem: The authors investigate whether perfect privacy can be achieved when multiple parties use quantum resource states, specifically Gaussian states, to perform distributed sensing.
main_result: They prove a no-go theorem showing that perfect privacy is impossible for any distributed sensing protocol utilizing Gaussian states. They instead introduce and analyze a measure of relative privacy.
method: The analysis uses necessary conditions derived from the requirement that the encoded state must only reveal information about the global function, not individual local parameters. This involves analyzing conditional states and Quantum Fisher Information (QFI).
model_or_system: The system models distributed sensing among N parties sharing a quantum resource state, focusing specifically on continuous variable Gaussian graph states.
key_observables: Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) matrix, the relative privacy measure ($R_{xy}$), and the encoded state $|\psi_{	ext{enc}}(\{	heta_i\})angle$.
important_parameters: The number of parties $N$, the structure of the graph state (e.g., fully-connected), and the transmissivity of loss channels.
main_assumptions: The analysis initially focuses on unitary encoding channels, though extensions to general channel encoding are discussed; perfect privacy is assumed impossible for Gaussian states.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the basic distributed sensing setup. Figure 3 shows how pairwise correlations can restore some form of privacy in an example setting.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing necessary conditions for private encoding (Theorem 2) to showing these fail for Gaussian states, and finally introduces relative privacy ($R_{xy}$) as a quantifiable measure of achievable information leakage.
why_interesting: This work provides fundamental theoretical limits on the security of quantum communication protocols in continuous variable settings, which is highly relevant for quantum sensing applications using optical resources.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: The basic setup for a distributed sensing problem. For privacy, we want to choose the parametrised unitaries, ui, so that the encoded state only holds information about a linear function of the parameters, and not their individual values.

FIG. 2: An illustration of the necessary condition for privacy stated in Theorem 2. If there exists a pair of unitaries, u and v, that collectively act as the identity, when applied to nodes 1 and 2, then u must act as the identity on all possible conditional states after tracing out node 2 and carrying out a measurement on all nodes except for 1 and 2.

FIG. 3: Privacy can be restored in a trivial way by allowing each pair of parties to establish pairwise correlations. This can be achieved if each party holds multiple nodes of a graph state, as illustrated here. If each party measures those of their nodes that are correlated with other nodes, they can use the outcomes to encode their remaining node in such a way that their secret parameter remains private.
